title: Free ISL football on YouTube pulled 65 million views in one week
subtitle: The Indian Super League put all 163 matches on YouTube for free. Here is how giving football away can still help a league earn.
content_html:
Picture this: 65 million plays of football videos in a single week, and not one fan had to pay a rupee to watch. That is what the Indian Super League (ISL) says happened in the opening week of its 2026-27 season on YouTube. The season kicked off on October 10, and The Economic Times reported the numbers on 16 October 2026.

So here is the big business question. If the matches are free, how does a football league make money? Grab a cup of chai. The answer is about one simple idea: reach.

What exactly happened in week one?

According to figures released by the league, the ISL got 65 million YouTube views and reached 52 million viewers across five matches in its first week.

A "view" is counted each time someone plays a video. One fan who watches the live match and then a highlights clip can add more than one view. That is why the number of viewers (52 million) is smaller than the number of views (65 million).

Some more numbers from the same report:

  • The most watched game on the English feed was NorthEast United FC against Mohun Bagan Super Giant, with 17 million views.
  • The opening match, Bengaluru FC against Sporting Club Delhi, got 8.9 million YouTube views.
  • Fans sent 1.6 million live interactions, such as chat messages and reactions.
  • The league's YouTube channel gained 120,000 new followers in the week, reaching 2.7 million in total.

Quick maths: 65 million views spread over five matches is an average of 13 million views per match. That is like filling a cricket stadium with 1 lakh people 130 times over, for every single game.

One honest warning. A report by Onmanorama points out that total views do not always mean unique viewers, or people who watched a full match. Views are a good sign of interest, not a head count.

Why was the football free in the first place?

Every big league sells "broadcast rights". This means a TV channel or app pays the league for the right to show its matches. It is a bit like a samosa stall owner paying rent to sell at the busiest corner of a fair.

This year, the ISL had a tough time. Onmanorama reports the league went months without a taker for its broadcast rights, and only found partners shortly before the season began.

The deal it finally made has three parts:

  • YouTube streams all 163 matches live and free.
  • Sony Sports Network is the league's exclusive TV broadcaster in India, and will show more than 80 matches on its channels.
  • SonyLIV also streams all 163 matches, on its paid platform.

The league calls this a digital-first approach, with every match open to fans without having to pay first.

Why would a league give its product away?

Think of a new ice cream shop that hands out free tasting spoons. The shop loses a little ice cream, but it gets a long line of people at the counter. Some of them will buy a cone, and many more will now know the shop's name.

Free football works in a similar way. The more people watch, the more valuable the league becomes to the companies that want to be seen by those people.

ISL CEO Karan Yadav said the league wants to be the most accessible league in the country. He also pointed to a big shift in how India watches: connected TV, which means a smart TV linked to the internet, has grown by 23% in a year to 166 million monthly viewers in India, he said.

So a fan can now open YouTube on the family smart TV and watch the ISL on the big screen, just like a normal TV channel, for free.

So where does the money come from?

A league like the ISL can earn in a few ways. Free streaming is meant to make each of them stronger.

1. Sponsors

A sponsor is a company that pays to put its name next to something people love. This season the league has a title sponsor again: JSW MG Motor India, the car maker. The league is now called the MG Indian Super League. A "title sponsor" gets its name in the league's own name, the way a cricket tournament might be named after a phone brand.

This is the first title sponsor in three seasons. Every extra million fans watching makes that name on the shirt and on the screen worth more.

2. TV and streaming deals

Sony still shows matches on TV and SonyLIV. A free YouTube stream and a paid TV channel can live side by side. Some fans like the big TV production; others are happy on a phone during a bus ride.

3. Ads and extra videos

Free videos online usually earn through ads, the short clips you see before or during a video. The ISL deal with YouTube also covers highlights, Shorts, interviews and behind-the-scenes videos. More videos mean more chances for fans to keep watching, and more space for brands.

The reports do not say how much money changes hands in the YouTube deal or the MG deal, so nobody outside the league can say yet how much each part earns.

The number advertisers really look at

Total views are nice. But brands also care about how many people are watching live, at the exact same moment. This is called "peak concurrent viewership". Think of it as the most people sitting in the stadium at one time, not the total number who walked in and out all day.

The biggest live crowd of the week on the English feed came for Inter Kashi against Kerala Blasters FC, at 349,073 people. The opening match peaked at 85,277 on the English feed, and NorthEast United against Mohun Bagan reached 100,660 on the Hindi feed.

Quick maths again: the Inter Kashi match had about four times the peak live crowd of the opening game. That shows how much interest can change from one match to the next.

Is the plan working?

Week one looks strong. But a football season is a long innings, not a single over. The season runs until May 31, 2027 with 13 teams.

The league has also planned for fans' free time. Of the 78 matches in the first phase, 53 are on Fridays, Saturdays or Sundays. That is about two out of every three games, timed for when students and young workers are free to watch.

As Onmanorama puts it, keeping the interest going all season is the next challenge. If the crowds stay, sponsors will notice. If they fade after the first few weeks, the free plan will look much less exciting.

The big lesson

In business, attention is a kind of money. The ISL is betting that free matches will bring in more fans, more fans will bring in more sponsors, and more sponsors will bring in more money for the league and its teams. Week one gave that bet a very good start.
